description:
We are a young team with a shared interest in space exploration.

We are enthusiasts who enjoy understanding how things work and sharing the knowledge we gain by creating educational content. Our skills include video design, website hosting, and the use of various web-based tools.

We use technology to explain how things—including equipment that is now obsolete—function. We do this through digital media, such as videos, 3D imagery, exploded-view diagrams, and interactive websites.
summary: Still Out Here (Sigo aquí) is a free, bilingual (English/Spanish) web story in which thirteen retired NASA machines tell their own story in the first person: the lunar landers and rover, the Viking landers, the Mars rovers and the Ingenuity helicopter, and the probes still out in deep space. For each one, visitors can take its 3D model apart piece by piece, learn what every part did and what science it made possible, follow its real journey drawn on NASA/JPL Horizons positions, and see where it rests or flies today. It answers the challenge "Abandoned but not Forgotten" by turning dense mission reports into stories that children, families and space fans remember, with every fact tied to a NASA source and everything illustrative honestly labelled. It matters because these machines are part of humanity's history, and a clear, accurate story is the best way to make people care about what we leave behind: on the Moon, on Mars and in orbit.
details:
What it does. The site tells the story of thirteen NASA machines grouped by where they are today. The Moon: Surveyor 3, Intrepid (the Apollo 12 lunar module and its ALSEP station) and the Apollo 15 lunar rover. Mars: the Viking landers, Sojourner, Spirit and Opportunity, Phoenix, InSight and the Ingenuity helicopter. Deep space: Pioneer 10 and 11, NEAR Shoemaker on asteroid Eros, Dawn at Ceres and the Kepler telescope around the Sun. Each one speaks in five chapters: Hello, My journey, How I'm built, What I found out, Where I am today.

  • Take it apart. A 3D model built from named parts (16 to 24 per machine, 236 in all) separates with a slider. Tapping a part, or choosing it from a list, explains what it is, what it did and what science it made possible. Historical states show how the hardware changed: Surveyor 3's TV camera and scoop appear as "ghosts" because the Apollo 12 astronauts took them back to Earth in 1969, and parts that failed are shown in red.
  • Real journeys. Paths are drawn on real NASA/JPL Horizons positions; Surveyor 3's flight and famous bouncing landing are keyframed from the 1967 JPL mission report. Where Horizons has no track (the Vikings, the Apollo 15 trip), an arc is drawn and the scene says it is illustrative.
  • Where it is today. Moon and Mars globes (NASA LRO, Viking and MOLA data) mark where each machine rests; for those still flying, live distances are computed from Horizons data.
  • "What if…?" An interactive 3D section on space debris: today's debris to NASA and ESA counts, the real 2009 Iridium 33 – Kosmos 2251 collision, and a clearly labelled toy model of a chain reaction in which visitors try 19 ideas (robotic arms, nets, harpoons, drag sails, lasers…), including ideas that do not work, explained with official figures. It closes the loop: none of our machines was left circling the Earth.
  • Hands-on science. A mini-experiment shows how Kepler found planets by measuring dips in starlight.

How it works and tools. It is a static web app with no server, built with JavaScript, three.js and Vite. Every 3D model is drawn in code from published dimensions, because NASA has no models of most of these machines. Every fact, part and date carries the NASA source it comes from, and we check that none is left without a source or a translation and that the models match the official dimensions. The journeys use real NASA/JPL Horizons positions. It is hosted on Cloudflare Workers. We used an AI assistant (Claude) for code, research, translation and checking; the demo video was composed with HyperFrames, with voice and music from HeyGen.

Benefits and intended impact. It brings forgotten hardware to life for school-age children and space fans, connects engineering to the science it enabled, and models good scientific practice: sources for every claim, honest labels for anything not to scale, predicted or illustrative, and the story of how scientists re-examined the "bacteria on the Moon" claim. It is free, needs no registration, and is built so a new spacecraft is added with one data file, one list of sources and one model; nine of the thirteen were added in a single day. We hope classrooms anywhere can visit the explorers that are still out there, and that people come away caring about the space we leave things in.

What is creative about it. The machines speak in the first person. You can take them apart and see what each piece did, including the pieces people took home and the ones that broke. The journeys use real NASA positions, not drawings. And the space-debris section lets visitors try to stop a chain reaction instead of just reading about one.

What our team considered.

  • Accuracy first: when NASA pages disagree (for example Surveyor 3's mass or Kepler's distance from Earth), the original mission report wins and the disagreement is shown in the "More detail" reading level.
  • Accessibility: built for people who are not used to computers (one big "Next" button, labelled buttons to turn and zoom the 3D view, a first-visit tip), with keyboard and screen-reader alternatives to the 3D canvas, a reduced-motion mode, two reading levels ("Simple" and "More detail"), two languages and a layout that works on phones.
  • Honesty: badges say when something is not to scale, is a JPL prediction or is an illustrative model.
  • Independence: this is an independent project, not endorsed by NASA; it uses no NASA logos or mission insignia.
  • Transparency about AI: the use of AI tools is declared on the site, in the code and in the demo video.
